raw_response:
I am still doing wheat-maize on all 10.9 mu. This land has fed my family for many years, and I do not want to take big risks. I cannot play with fancy methods. I do what has worked on my fields and what the other good farmers around here do. Wheat needs to stand strong through winter and spring, so I will not save too much on base fertilizer. Maize comes right after wheat, and the time is tight, so I will keep the land work simple and sow fast. Water from the well helps, but pumping costs money, so I will use it at the important times, not carelessly. If I spend too little on fertilizer, I am afraid the crop will turn yellow and lose yield; if I spend too much, I waste money. So I will stay around the middle, same as a steady year.

For wheat, I will sow in early October on the whole 10.9 mu after the maize is off. I will use the common wheat seed sold locally, the kind people here usually buy, not anything strange. Before sowing I will put most of the fertilizer down, then add some urea later if the wheat looks like it needs feeding around jointing. I will water about three times if the season is normal: one after sowing or before winter if the soil is dry, one at jointing, and one at filling if needed. For maize, I will plant right after wheat harvest in June, on the same 10.9 mu. I will use hybrid maize seed because local hybrids yield better and most people around here use them. I will hurry the turnaround, do only light rotary tillage or direct seeding after wheat, and topdress once after emergence when the maize is growing strongly. If summer rain is decent, I may only irrigate once; if rain is good enough, I can skip that one to save pumping money.
